summary: This informational document explains how the Access Node Control Mechanism applies to broadband access built on Passive Optical Networks (PONs). It covers a network access server working with an access node made of Optical Line Termination and Optical Network Termination elements. The mechanism supports QoS-related, service-related, and subscriber-related operations.

plainLanguage.summary: Fiber internet has boxes at the street and at homes. This explains how the main control box can talk to those boxes to manage service.

questions: access node control mechanism for pon
how does ancp work with pon
subtitle: Control protocol for fiber broadband networks based on passive optical networks.

tldr.problem: Fiber-based broadband networks (PON) need real-time coordination between the central office equipment and the network access server to manage quality of service, provision services, and enable multicast video delivery across the access network.
tldr.mechanism: The Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP) is extended to allow a Network Access Server to communicate directly with PON equipment (OLT and ONT) for QoS control, multicast admission control, and topology discovery without requiring separate element managers.
tldr.outcome: Broadband providers can deliver triple-play services (voice, video, data) over fiber with coordinated, near-real-time control that meets performance objectives.

today: RFC 6934 is an Informational document published in June 2013 that extends the Access Node Control Protocol framework to PON deployments. The protocol and its application to fiber broadband networks remain relevant to modern broadband deployments leveraging optical access technology.

sections.title: PON-Based Broadband Networks
sections.content:
Passive Optical Networks (PONs) based on BPON, GPON, and XG-PON are being deployed as next-generation broadband access. Unlike traditional copper-based broadband, PONs offer dramatically higher bandwidth: BPON provides 622 Mbit/s, GPON provides 2.4 Gbit/s, and XG-PON provides 10 Gbit/s. PON deployments come in two models: Fiber to the Building/Curb (FTTB/FTTC), where fiber extends to a neighborhood node and copper extends the last mile to premises, and Fiber to the Premises (FTTP), where fiber goes all the way to the subscriber premises.

Broadband providers use PONs to deliver triple-play services: voice (VoIP), video (both multicast broadcast and on-demand), and data. Each service has different requirements. Voice requires low delay and packet loss; video requires low jitter and bandwidth allocation; data requires throughput. Coordinating these services across the access network requires tight, near-real-time control between the central office equipment and the subscriber management platform.
sections.plainLanguage: PON is super fast fiber that can deliver TV, phone calls, and internet together. The network needs to talk between the office and the street to make sure each service gets the right speed and quality.

sections.title: Network Architecture and Components
sections.content:
A PON-based broadband access network has several key components. At the subscriber premises is a Home Gateway (HGW) that connects subscriber devices to the network. The Optical Network Terminal (ONT) or Optical Network Unit (ONU) terminates the fiber and adapts it for the subscriber interface. The Optical Line Terminal (OLT), located in the central office, terminates and aggregates multiple PONs. The Network Access Server (NAS), also called a Broadband Network Gateway or BRAS, aggregates subscriber traffic and is the injection point for policy, QoS, and subscriber management.

The fundamental difference between PON and DSL is that PON is a broadcast network: every device on the same PON sees the same signal. The ONT filters only frames addressed to it. This broadcast capability makes PON excellent for multicast video delivery, where one stream on the PON can reach multiple subscribers with one copy of the data.
sections.plainLanguage: The street box (OLT) sends signals down the fiber to your home box (ONT). The office computer (NAS) talks to the street box to manage what service you get.

sections.title: Access Node Control Protocol for PON
sections.content:
The Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP) is a transactional protocol that enables direct device-to-device communication between the NAS and the Access Node Complex (the OLT and ONT together) without requiring separate element managers. This allows access-link-related operations within the network elements to meet performance objectives.

ANCP in PON environments supports several key use cases: Access topology discovery lets the NAS learn the structure of the PON and its devices; Access loop configuration lets the NAS configure parameters of the subscriber access line; Remote connectivity check lets the NAS verify that a subscriber's connection is working; and Multicast admission control coordinates bandwidth allocation for multicast video between the NAS and the ANX.

ANCP can also be used between components of the Access Node Complex itself (between the OLT and ONT) to provide control that would normally require separate management systems.
sections.plainLanguage: ANCP is a rule for how the office computer talks to the street box and the home box to control service without needing a separate control system.

sections.title: Multicast Video and Admission Control
sections.content:
Enabling multicast on the Access Node Complex provides bandwidth efficiency on the path between the access node and the NAS and reduces the load on the NAS by preventing it from having to replicate the same video stream for each subscriber. PON's broadcast capability allows the OLT to send one copy of a multicast stream on the PON, where every connected subscriber can receive it.

The OLT can assign no encryption key, a single key for all multicast channels, or a key per service package to control which subscribers see which channels. The OLT sends encryption keys to each targeted ONT via the ONT Management and Control Interface (OMCI).

ANCP provides multicast admission control, allowing coordinated decisions about which multicast streams are admitted to the network, with multicast accounting to track usage, and multicast conditional access to control which subscribers receive which services.
sections.plainLanguage: PON can send one copy of a TV show to everyone on the fiber, saving bandwidth. ANCP helps decide who gets to watch what based on their service package.

sections.title: Security and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
PON uses encryption on the fiber to prevent eavesdropping, with encryption keys managed by the OLT and distributed to ONTs. The document notes security considerations related to various methods of dealing with multicast access control and encryption, though it does not propose methods for securing ANCP itself in the PON context.

The key architectural difference between PON and DSL is that DSL is point-to-point while PON is point-to-multipoint. This affects how ANCP is applied: in DSL, multicast is enabled only on the DSL Access Multiplexer (DSLAM), while in PON, multicast must be enabled on both the OLT and ONT to take advantage of the broadcast capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Fiber signal is encrypted so people cannot intercept it. The system needs to decide which boxes get which encryption keys.
